result.topic_en: This spread (pp. 264–265) finishes a proof that a^p − 1 is divisible by 2p+1 when a is a quadratic residue, and gives a corollary on residues larger than the divisor. It then tabulates quadratic residues for the primes 3 to 37 and states Theorem 8, which says for which primes 2p+1 the number 11^p − 1 or 11^p + 1 is divisible.

items.quote: Ex quo ſequitur, etiam poteſtatem $a^p$ vnitatem relinquere, ſiue formulam $a^p-1$ eſſe diuiſibilem.
items.english: From which it follows that the power a^p also leaves remainder one, i.e. that the formula a^p − 1 is divisible.

items.quote: Cum reſidua $1$; $\alpha$; $\beta$; $\gamma$; $\delta$; etc. minora eſſe ſoleant quam diuiſor $2p+1$; iis adhuc annumerari licet $1+(2p+1)$; $\alpha+(2p+1)$; $\beta+(2p+1)$; etc.
items.english: Since the residues 1, α, β, γ, δ, etc. are usually smaller than the divisor 2p+1, one may also count among them 1+(2p+1), α+(2p+1), β+(2p+1), etc.

items.quote: Sumto $a=11$, ſi fuerit $2p+1$ numerus primus, vtrum per eum diuiſibilis ſit formula $11^p-1$, ſiue $11^p+1$, ſequens tabella oſtendit.
items.english: Taking a = 11, if 2p+1 is a prime number, the following table shows whether the formula 11^p − 1 or 11^p + 1 is divisible by it.
